claim: Many species use social networks to buffer the effects of stress.
source: Many species use social networks to buffer the effects of stress.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific knowledge about social buffering of stress across species.

claim: Social isolation alters the intrinsic properties of PVN CRH neurons in sexually dimorphic fashion.
source: We examined neuroendocrine, PVN CRH neurons and report that social isolation alters the intrinsic properties of these cells in sexually dimorphic fashion.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Isolating preadolescent female mice from littermates for <24 hr increased first spike latency (FSL) of CRH neurons.
source: Specifically, isolating preadolescent female mice from littermates for <24 hr increased first spike latency (FSL) and decreased excitability of CRH neurons.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1.

claim: Isolating preadolescent female mice from littermates for <24 hr decreased excitability of CRH neurons.
source: Specifically, isolating preadolescent female mice from littermates for <24 hr increased first spike latency (FSL) and decreased excitability of CRH neurons.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 5.

claim: Changes in FSL and excitability following social isolation were not evident in age-matched males.
source: These changes were not evident in age-matched males.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing males and females in Figure 1.

claim: Subjecting single-housed males to acute physical stress (swim) increased FSL.
source: By contrast, subjecting either males (isolated or grouped) or group housed females to acute physical stress (swim), increased FSL.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Subjecting group-housed males to acute physical stress (swim) increased FSL.
source: By contrast, subjecting either males (isolated or grouped) or group housed females to acute physical stress (swim), increased FSL.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Subjecting group-housed females to acute physical stress (swim) increased FSL.
source: By contrast, subjecting either males (isolated or grouped) or group housed females to acute physical stress (swim), increased FSL.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The increase in FSL following social isolation was blocked by the glucocorticoid synthesis inhibitor, metyrapone.
source: The increase in FSL following either social isolation or acute physical stress was blocked by the glucocorticoid synthesis inhibitor, metyrapone and mimicked by exogenous corticosterone.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The increase in FSL following acute physical stress was blocked by the glucocorticoid synthesis inhibitor, metyrapone.
source: The increase in FSL following either social isolation or acute physical stress was blocked by the glucocorticoid synthesis inhibitor, metyrapone and mimicked by exogenous corticosterone.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The increase in FSL following social isolation was mimicked by exogenous corticosterone.
source: The increase in FSL following either social isolation or acute physical stress was blocked by the glucocorticoid synthesis inhibitor, metyrapone and mimicked by exogenous corticosterone.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The increase in FSL following acute physical stress was mimicked by exogenous corticosterone.
source: The increase in FSL following either social isolation or acute physical stress was blocked by the glucocorticoid synthesis inhibitor, metyrapone and mimicked by exogenous corticosterone.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Social isolation, but not acute physical stress has sex-specific effects on PVN CRH neurons.
source: Our observations demonstrate that social isolation, but not acute physical stress has sex-specific effects on PVN CRH neurons.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion supported by the experimental data comparing males and females under different stress conditions.

claim: Survival threats trigger a repertoire of behavioral and endocrine adjustments.
source: Survival threats trigger a repertoire of behavioral and endocrine adjustments (Cannon, 1932).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cannon, 1932.

claim: The endocrine changes in response to survival threats rely on the immediate engagement of the hypothalamic pituitary adrenal (HPA) axis.
source: The endocrine changes rely on the immediate engagement of the hypothalamic pituitary adrenal (HPA) axis which is controlled by corticotropin releasing hormone (CRH) neurons in the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus (PVN).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the HPA axis.

claim: The HPA axis is controlled by corticotropin releasing hormone (CRH) neurons in the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus (PVN).
source: The endocrine changes rely on the immediate engagement of the hypothalamic pituitary adrenal (HPA) axis which is controlled by corticotropin releasing hormone (CRH) neurons in the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus (PVN).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the HPA axis.

claim: Dysregulation of the stress response is implicated in the emergence of numerous neuropsychiatric diseases.
source: Although it is essential for survival, the dysregulation of the stress response is implicated in the emergence of numerous neuropsychiatric diseases (Tost et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tost et al., 2015.

claim: Many neuropsychiatric diseases show sex-specific differences.
source: Interestingly, many of these psychopathologies show sex-specific differences which may be a consequence of sexual dimorphism of the neuroendocrine response to stress (Bale and Epperson, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bale and Epperson, 2015.

claim: Sex-specific differences in neuropsychiatric diseases may be a consequence of sexual dimorphism of the neuroendocrine response to stress.
source: Interestingly, many of these psychopathologies show sex-specific differences which may be a consequence of sexual dimorphism of the neuroendocrine response to stress (Bale and Epperson, 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by a citation.

claim: Young girls exhibit greater corticosteroid (CORT) stress reactivity to social stress tests than boys.
source: Human studies demonstrating that young girls exhibit greater corticosteroid (CORT) stress reactivity to social stress tests than boys (Gunnar et al., 2009; de Veld et al., 2012) suggest, for example, that young females are more responsive to changes in social situations.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gunnar et al., 2009 and de Veld et al., 2012.

claim: Young females are more responsive to changes in social situations than young males.
source: Human studies demonstrating that young girls exhibit greater corticosteroid (CORT) stress reactivity to social stress tests than boys (Gunnar et al., 2009; de Veld et al., 2012) suggest, for example, that young females are more responsive to changes in social situations.

claim: Females take greater advantage of social support and group dynamics to manage stress in comparison to males.
source: Consistent with this idea, are demonstrations that, in comparison to males, females take greater advantage of social support and group dynamics to manage stress (Taylor et al., 2000).

claim: Mice were housed in same-sex groups (3–5 animals per group) from weaning (p21) until the day of the experiment (p22–35).
source: To test this idea, mice were housed in same-sex groups (3–5 animals per group) from weaning (p21) until the day of the experiment (p22–35).
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol used in the study.

claim: The developmental window p22-35 allows interrogation of sex differences independent of the effects of circulating gonadal hormones.
source: This developmental window allows us to interrogate the contributions of sex differences independent of the effects of circulating gonadal hormones (Nelson et al., 1990).

claim: Activation of PVN CRH neurons is obligatory for launching the neuroendocrine response to stress.
source: Activation of these cells is obligatory for launching the neuroendocrine response to stress (Denver, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Denver, 2009.

claim: Social isolation had no effect on FSL in males (malegroup: 48.7 ± 2.1 ms, n = 53 vs malesingle: 46.1 ± 1.8 ms, n = 76, p=0.9).

claim: FSL in isolated females was significantly longer than FSL in group-housed females (femalegroup: 45.1 ± 1.9 ms, n = 42; femalesingle: 65.6 ± 1.9, n = 177, p<0.0001).

claim: Pair-housed females exhibited FSLs that were longer than those observed in group housed female mice, but shorter than those observed in single-housed female mice (femalepaired: 56.5 ± 2.0 ms, n = 105, p=0.0029 vs femalesingle and p=0.0017 vs femalegroup).
source: This manipulation revealed an intermediate phenotype, with pair-housed females exhibiting FSLs that were longer than those observed in group housed female mice, but shorter than those observed in single-housed female mice (femalepaired: 56.5 ± 2.0 ms, n = 105, p=0.0029 vs femalesingle and p=0.0017 vs femalegroup, F4,471 = 10.6).

source: There was no difference in the input resistance of isolated males vs isolated females (malesingle: 796 ± 31 MΩ, n = 157, vs femalesingle: 869 ± 23 MΩ, n = 273; unpaired t-test, p=0.063; Figure 1—figure supplement 1)

claim: There was no difference in spike threshold between isolated males and isolated females (malesingle: −51.5 ± 1.0 mV, n = 63 vs femalesingle: −51.3 ± 0.7 mV, n = 99; unpaired t-test, p=0.86).
source: or spike threshold (malesingle: −51.5 ± 1.0 mV, n = 63 vs femalesingle: −51.3 ± 0.7 mV, n = 99; unpaired t-test, p=0.86; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

claim: There were no differences in basal glutamate synaptic transmission between single-housed females and males.

claim: There were no differences in basal GABA synaptic transmission between single-housed females and males.
source: We also examined properties of glutamate and GABA synapses on CRH neurons in hypothalamic slices from single-housed females and males. We observed no differences in basal glutamate (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) or GABA (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) synaptic transmission.

claim: Following swim stress, FSL in male mice (maleswim) was 64.0 ± 4.6 ms, n = 37, which is significantly longer than FSL in single males not subjected to swim (p=0.0004).
source: Following swim stress, FSL in male mice (maleswim) was 64.0 ± 4.6 ms, n = 37, Figure 2b,c; this is significantly longer than FSL in the single males reported above (maleswim vs malesingle, 1 way ANOVA, p=0.0004).

claim: FSL in single female mice subjected to swim stress was 65.8 ± 4.9 ms, n = 32, which is not different from FSL in female mice subjected to social isolation (p=0.67).
source: FSL in single female mice subjected to swim stress was 65.8 ± 4.9 ms, n = 32, Figure 2b,c; this is not different from FSL in female mice subjected to social isolation (femaleswim vs femalesingle, p=0.67).

claim: FSL in single males subjected to swim was not different from FSL in single females subjected to swim (p=0.9).
source: Finally, FSL in single males subjected to swim was not different from FSL in single females subjected to swim (p=0.9, Figure 2b,c).

claim: Following swim, FSL in group-housed males (malegroup swim: 58.8 ± 2.8 ms, n = 23) was significantly longer than FSL in naïve, group-housed males (p<0.001).
source: Following swim, FSL in group-housed males (malegroup swim: 58.8 ± 2.8 ms, n = 23, Figure 2d) was significantly longer than FSL in naïve, group -housed males (p<0.001).

claim: FSL of group-housed males subjected to swim was not different than FSL in females subjected to swim (femalegroup swim:58.7 ± 1.9 ms, n = 27, p>0.05 vs malegroup).
source: FSL of group-housed males subjected to swim was not different than FSL in females subjected to swim (femalegroup swim:58.7 ± 1.9 ms, n = 27, p>0.05 vs malegroup, Figure 2d).

claim: Metyrapone treatment blocked the effects of social isolation on FSL in female mice (femalesingle metyrapone = 47.2 ± 2.0 ms, n = 24, p=0.001 vs femalesingle).

claim: CORT is necessary for stress-induced changes in FSL in both males and females.

evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the metyrapone experiments.

claim: CORT-incubation increased FSL in slices from single-housed males (59.2 ± 4.1 ms, n = 36, p<0.021 vs malesingle).
source: CORT-incubation increased FSL in slices from single-housed males (59.2 ± 4.1 ms, n = 36, p<0.021 vs malesingle) and in slices from group-housed females (64.1 ± 4.8 ms, n = 32, p<0.0001 vs femalegroup, Figure 3f).

claim: CORT-incubation increased FSL in slices from group-housed females (64.1 ± 4.8 ms, n = 32, p<0.0001 vs femalegroup).

evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in the text and Figure 3f.

claim: CORT is both necessary (during stress) and sufficient (in the absence of stress) to increase FSL in male and female mice.

claim: Rapidly activating and inactivating K currents are sensitive to millimolar concentrations of 4-aminopyridine (4-AP).
source: Rapidly activating and inactivating K currents are sensitive to millimolar concentrations of 4-aminopyridine (4-AP) (Alexander et al., 2015), and consistent with this, we observed shorter FSL in the presence of 2 mM 4-AP (FSL4-AP: 36.8 ± 5.6 ms vs FSLcontrol: 62.8 ± 7.6 ms unpaired t-test, p=0.015 n = 8, Figure 4a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Alexander et al., 2015 and experimental data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: FSL was shorter in the presence of 2 mM 4-AP (FSL4-AP: 36.8 ± 5.6 ms vs FSLcontrol: 62.8 ± 7.6 ms unpaired t-test, p=0.015 n = 8).
source: Rapidly activating and inactivating K currents are sensitive to millimolar concentrations of 4-aminopyridine (4-AP) (Alexander et al., 2015), and consistent with this, we observed shorter FSL in the presence of 2 mM 4-AP (FSL4-AP: 36.8 ± 5.6 ms vs FSLcontrol: 62.8 ± 7.6 ms unpaired t-test, p=0.015 n = 8, Figure 4a).

claim: The rapidly activating K currents in CRH neurons inactivated quickly.
source: These currents were largely inactive at resting membrane potential, inactivated quickly and required membrane hyperpolarization to relieve inactivation (Figure 4b).

claim: The rapidly activating K currents were fully blocked by 6 mM 4-AP (n = 4).

This is revealed as a rightward shift in the relationship between spike probability and current step (female: I50 = 49.5 ± 1.2 mV, n = 104 vs male: I50 = 55.0 ± 1.6 mV, n = 88, p<0.0001, K-S statistic).
